analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice damages for obstetric and gynecological care at $250,000 for pain and suffering and restricts lawsuits against doctors and hospitals.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on January 10, 2007, received no hearing or vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for lawsuits over injuries from pregnancy and women's health care. It capped compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 per provider ($500,000 total from hospitals), cut lawyers' contingency fees, tightened expert-witness rules, barred most punitive damages, and reduced awards by the amount of any insurance benefits the patient received. Its stated goal was to lower malpractice insurance costs so more obstetricians keep practicing and women keep access to maternity care.
analysis.who_benefits: Obstetricians, gynecologists, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers, whose liability exposure and insurance premiums would fall. Patients would keep unlimited recovery for out-of-pocket losses like medical bills and lost wages, but the ceiling on pain-and-suffering awards would fall hardest on patients with severe injuries whose main loss is not financial.

how_it_helps.text: Supporters argued the liability system was driving obstetricians out of childbirth care, citing the finding in the bill that one in seven OB-GYNs had stopped practicing obstetrics [S3].
The bill kept recovery of economic damages — medical bills, lost earnings, and other verifiable losses — fully unlimited [S2].
It required courts to sanction frivolous lawsuits and set stricter qualifications for expert witnesses, which supporters said would screen out weak claims [S2].
It limited lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale starting at 40 percent of the first $50,000, leaving more of any award with the patient [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Women and infants injured by negligent obstetric or gynecological care, whose compensation for pain, suffering, disfigurement, and loss of a child would be capped, and whose awards would be reduced by insurance benefits they were already entitled to receive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients injured by negligent maternity care

drawbacks.text: The bill would have preempted state law nationwide, overriding state tort rules that currently govern medical malpractice cases, including states that provide greater compensation [S3].

Capping noneconomic damages at $250,000 most reduces compensation for the most seriously injured — babies with lifelong birth injuries and women disfigured or disabled by negligence — while leaving overall liability savings uncertain, since economic damages remain uncapped [S2].
Reducing awards by collateral source benefits means a patient's own insurance could effectively shrink her recovery, shifting costs back onto the injured person [S2].

The bill would bar naming a doctor as a defendant in product liability suits over FDA-approved drugs or devices prescribed for approved uses, narrowing remedies when a harmful prescription causes injury [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded a real, immediate reduction in malpractice exposure for doctors and insurers against an unproven promise of better access to maternity care and a certain reduction in compensation for the most severely injured patients. Evidence on whether damage caps materially expand access to obstetric care is mixed, while the loss of compensation for catastrophically injured babies and mothers is concrete and permanent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on its first day, and the committee never acted on it, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg of New Hampshire introduced the bill on January 10, 2007, the opening day of the 110th Congress, joined by 12 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action appears in the record for the next two years [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients and trial lawyers kept the existing liability system, with no national cap on compensation for injured mothers and babies; physicians and malpractice insurers gained nothing. With Democrats holding the Senate majority and the Judiciary chairmanship, a bill with no Democratic support was never going to advance, and it did not.

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 110th Congress and assembled a Republican cosponsor group.

for.name: 12 of 49 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, including Sen. Mitch McConnell and Sen. John Cornyn; all twelve were Republicans.

against.name: Sen. Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: The committee to which the bill was referred never held a hearing or markup, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Provided no cosponsors for the bill and controlled the committee agenda where it was referred.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support in either the sponsorship or any recorded action; medical malpractice caps were a longstanding Republican priority opposed by most Democrats.

industries.note: Caps on damages and restrictions on lawsuits directly reduce the claims insurers must pay. The benefit comes out of compensation otherwise owed to injured patients.

Doctors and hospitals would face lower liability exposure and, supporters argued, lower insurance premiums that could preserve access to maternity care. Their gain is the mirror image of injured patients' capped recoveries.

Sliding-scale contingency fee caps, mandatory sanctions, and strict expert-witness rules reduce both the volume and the profitability of malpractice suits, which are how patients finance legal representation.

The bill shields any provider who prescribed an FDA-approved product from being named in product liability or class action suits, making it harder to pull prescribing physicians into litigation over harmful products.
